opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single moment. It was more a slow accumulation of doubt.

During the early part of my PhD at Tsinghua, I worked on fairly classic machine-learning problems: transfer learning, model selection, how to reuse pretrained models more effectively. The typical workflow was that you'd find a benchmark, propose a method, and if you could push accuracy up by one or two points, you'd write a paper. For a while that felt meaningful. You learn a lot, you get publications, and the community rewards it.

But over time I began to feel uneasy. Many of those improvements were fragile. They worked on a particular dataset under particular settings, and when the next, bigger pretrained model came out, a lot of the clever tricks simply stopped mattering. The gains got washed away by scale. I'd spend months on an idea, and then a new foundation model would arrive and the whole problem would look different. That's a very humbling experience as a researcher.

Then ChatGPT came out, and it was a real shock. It made it very clear to me that the center of gravity in the field had shifted. The most important questions were no longer about squeezing out another point on a benchmark. They were about how to train, serve, and use these huge models, and who could actually run them.

I also noticed something about myself. I've always liked building systems and writing code that people actually use, more than polishing a method for a leaderboard. With large models, the bottleneck very obviously moved toward systems: memory, throughput, latency, cost. Inference in particular was becoming a huge problem, because once a model is useful, everyone wants to run it, and it's incredibly expensive.

So I started spending time at Berkeley and getting involved in open-source inference work, which eventually became my main focus with vLLM. That felt like a much more direct way to have impact. If you make inference faster or cheaper, that benefit goes to everyone using these models, not just to a number in a table.

So in short, it was partly disillusionment with incremental accuracy work, partly the shock of seeing what large models could do, and partly realizing that my own interests and skills fit better on the systems side, where the real bottlenecks now were.

r002.rationale: It says earlier improvements were fragile and often stopped mattering when larger models arrived. It does not clearly state that the research was unsuitable for application at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from a kind of frustration. During my PhD at Tsinghua, I was working on transfer learning and domain adaptation, and the whole field had settled into a rhythm: you propose a new loss, you get maybe half a point better on Office-31 or DomainNet, you write the paper, and then next year someone else gets another half point. I did that for a few years. The papers got accepted, but I started asking myself whether anyone outside our small circle would ever use any of it. The answer, mostly, was no.

Then around 2022 it became obvious that scale was doing what our clever tricks were supposed to do. A pretrained model with enough data was simply more robust to distribution shift than anything we were hand-crafting. That was a bit painful, because it meant a lot of the problem I had been studying was being dissolved rather than solved. But it also clarified things. If the bottleneck was no longer the algorithm but the ability to actually train and serve these models, then the leverage was in systems.

So I shifted toward infrastructure, and eventually that led me to vLLM. What attracted me is that inference is where models meet real users. If you make serving twice as fast or half as expensive, every single person running that model benefits immediately, and you can measure it. That felt much more real than a benchmark number.

I also think my background wasn't wasted. Years of debugging training pipelines and reading PyTorch internals turned out to be exactly what you need when you're wiring a new model architecture into a serving engine, or figuring out why CUDA graphs break on some edge case. The skills transferred, even if the research questions didn't.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated half-point benchmark gains and marginal impact, but does not characterize the work as polishing solutions to tasks others had already accomplished.

r002.rationale: You says that mostly nobody outside the research circle used the incremental work, and that sufficiently scaled pretrained models were more robust than the hand-crafted approaches, making the earlier research ineffective for broader practical use.

astra-6.text:
For me, it was a shift in the question I wanted to work on. When you focus on improving accuracy on a particular benchmark, the task is already defined, and you’re trying to make the model a little better at it. That’s useful, but I became more interested in whether a model could handle a broader range of tasks—and what would make that possible.

Large models offered a way to explore that question. They also made the practical side harder to ignore: how you train them, how you run them efficiently, and how you make them useful. So I started thinking less about one accuracy number and more about the capabilities of the whole system.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was a gradual change in what I thought was an important research question. When you work on improving accuracy, you often start with a fixed task and a fixed benchmark, and then ask how to make the model a little better. That can be useful, but I became more interested in whether we could expand what a model could do in the first place.

Large models made that question much more compelling. You could use the same model for many different tasks, sometimes just by changing the instructions. So my attention shifted from optimizing performance on one benchmark toward understanding these broader capabilities—and the practical challenges of making them useful. It wasn’t that accuracy stopped mattering; it became one part of a much larger problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes improving a fixed task and benchmark, but does not say others had already accomplished those tasks or characterize the work as polishing existing solutions.

r002.rationale: It mentions practical challenges of making large models useful, but does not say his earlier incremental-accuracy research was unsuitable for application at scale.
